code: size_t count = cs_disasm(handle, Data+1, Size-1, address, 0, &all_insn);
note: The fuzzer-controlled bytes after the platform selector are supplied to the real Capstone disassembler; for this candidate they are opcode 0x02 and ModR/M 0xc0.
The input byte 0x02 is consumed as the one-byte x86 opcode used for table lookup.
The input byte 0xc0 is consumed as the ModR/M byte; mod == 3 selects the register-register form of opcode 0x02.
Decoding opcode 0x02 with ModR/M 0xc0 returns the internal instruction id for ADD8rr_REV.
The decoded internal id is copied into the MCInst opcode that later drives public-id mapping and printing.

code: unsigned int i = find_insn(insns, ARR_SIZE(insns), id);
note: The safety obligation is that every printable internal opcode must have a mapping entry; ADD8rr_REV is absent, so find_insn returns -1 and leaves insn->id as the uninitialized value from the heap-allocated cs_insn cache.
Because the mapping lookup failed, this call does not initialize the public instruction id field in the cached output instruction.
The Intel printer is invoked for the decoded instruction, matching the vulnerable crash state before the fuzz target prints the completed cs_insn.
The fuzz target reads the uninitialized public instruction id and passes it to cs_insn_name, triggering MemorySanitizer's use-of-uninitialized-value report.
